mechaber.en:
Damage by an animal's foot and its derivatives, the laws of pebbles, and a dog or rooster that jumped. It contains twelve seifim:
Regel, damage caused by an animal's normal walking, is a primary category of damages, as expressed in the Torah's phrase concerning letting one's animal loose. It occurs when an animal walks with its feet and causes damage in the normal course of walking, where this is its usual manner and the animal derives no benefit from the act. Anything similar is a derivative and has the same law. Thus, if it damages with its body while walking, with its hair, with a load-sack Bartenura explains in the first chapter of Bava Kamma that this means burdens carried in sacks and packs upon it, with the bridle meaning a rein in its mouth, with the bell on its neck, or with the load on its back; or if chickens fly from place to place and break utensils with their wings; or if they tread and dance meaning trampling and hopping on dough or fruit and soil it, or peck at it; or anything attached to the animal's body causes damage, such as a wagon being pulled over utensils and breaking them, all these are derivatives of regel and have its law.

turei_zahav.he: (ס"ב) וי"א דבכל ספק דין כו'. מה שתירץ בסמ"ע דקנס שאני הוא תמוה מאד חדא מנין לטור לחלק בזה ואדרבה נראה שאין חילוק כיון דתפוס וחייב קנס מדין תורה א"כ למה לא יזכה מכח ממ"נ מדין תורה. ותו דלפי דבריו אין דין זה מקושר שם דעת הרא"ש וסידור דברי הטור לא משמע כן אלא שייך דוקא לדעת הרא"ש ונ"ל דהא תליא בספק דינא אי מהני תפיסה דהרמ"ה ס"ל דתפיסה מועיל לספיקא דדינא וכן מוכרח בסימן רמ"ב ס"ס ג' להרמ"ה דמהני תפיסה בספק דין וכרמב"ם ומ"ה לא כליא זכותא דהלוקח שם דהא אף בספק הראשון יש לו כח לתפוס המוכר ע"כ האידנא שנולד ספק שני אתא עליה מכח ממ"נ ואפי' לא תפיס מהני שיתן לו אחד מהם אבל כאן דקיימינן לדעת ר"י והרא"ש דבספק דין לא מהני תפיסה מ"ה אחר שנולד הספק הא' לא היה שום אפשרות ביד הניזק להשתלם מן המזיק כמו שהוא חפץ ע"כ נתבטל אותו החיוב כאלו לא היה וכי נולד אח"כ הספק הב' הוי כאלו הוא לבדו ולא קדמו ספק אחר וע"כ סמך הטור דבר זה לדעת הרא"ש ודבר זה הוא דומה למאי דאמרינן בפ' החולץ דף ל"ז בספק ויבם דקם דינא ולא מהני שם ממ"נ כנ"ל נכון:
turei_zahav.en: [Seif 2] Some say that in every unresolved legal question, and so forth. The Sema's answer, that a penalty is different, is exceedingly difficult. First, what source does the Tur have for such a distinction? On the contrary, there should be no distinction. Since the claimant is in possession and the defendant is liable for the penalty under Torah law, why should the claimant not prevail by a Torah-law argument of “either way”? Second, according to the Sema, this ruling is not connected to the Rosh's opinion where the Tur places it, whereas the arrangement of the Tur clearly indicates that it applies specifically according to the Rosh. It appears to me that the matter depends on the general question whether possession is effective in a legal doubt. The Ramah holds that possession is effective in an unresolved question of law, as is necessarily evident at the end of siman 242, seif 3, where his position accords with the Rambam. Therefore, the purchaser's right in that case was not extinguished by the first doubt, because even then he could retain money from the seller. When a second doubt later arose, he may assert an “either way” claim, and even without prior possession it is sufficient that one of the two parties pay him. Here, however, we are following Rabbeinu Yitzchak and the Rosh, who hold that possession does not help in a legal doubt. Once the first doubt arose, the injured party had no possibility of collecting from the tortfeasor as he wished, and that obligation was therefore extinguished as though it had never existed. When the second doubt later arose, it is treated as standing alone, without a prior doubt to create an “either way” claim. The Tur therefore placed this ruling specifically after the Rosh's view. This resembles the rule in Yevamot 37b concerning a doubtful son and a yavam, where the prior judgment stands and an “either way” claim does not help. This appears correct.

mechaber.he: כשכשה בזנבה כשכוש רב שאין דרכה לעשות תמיד והזיקה ברשות הרבים או שכשכשה בגיד שלה ברשות הרבים והזיקה פטור ואם תפס הניזק גובה חצי נזק ממה שתפס שזה הדבר ספק הוא אם אלו תולדות הקרן שחייב עליה ברשות הרבים או תולדות הרגל שפטור עליה ברשות הרבים: הגה וי"א דבכל ספקא דדינא לא מהני תפיסה ולכן אפי' אם תפס מפקינן מיניה (טור ס"א בשם ר"י ) (וע"ל סי' שכ"א) ולדעת הרא"ש דכשכשה בזנבה לא הוי ספק ודאי פטור (טור שם הביאו):
mechaber.en: If an animal repeatedly and unusually lashes with its tail and causes damage in the public domain, or lashes with its male organ in the public domain and causes damage, the owner is exempt. If the injured party seized property, he may collect half-damages from what he seized, because there is an unresolved question whether these acts are derivatives of horn, for which liability applies in the public domain, or derivatives of foot, for which there is exemption there. Rama: Some hold that seizure is ineffective in every unresolved question of law, and therefore even if the injured party seized property it is removed from him. According to Rosh, lashing with the tail is not doubtful at all and the owner is certainly exempt.

baer_hetev.he: דדינא. היינו בבעיא דלא איפשטא ובזה מודים דאם הזיקה ברשות הניזק דאינו משלם כלל אא"כ תפס גוף המזיק דוקא ואז ישלם ממנו ח"נ דכיון דלא איפשטא י"ל דלא הוי אורחה ותולדה דקרן הוא וקרן אינו משלם אלא ח"נ מגופו והטור מסיק בזה וכת' וז"ל ואפילו אם הזיק לאדם אחד בר"ה וברשות הניזק דינא הכי וא"י לו' ממ"נ אם תאמר שהוא קרן תתחייב לי ג"כ בר"ה וא"ת שהוא רגל תן לי נ"ש היזקא דרשות הניזק אלא בשניהן להקל עכ"ל ואע"ג דבסי' ר' כת' הטור גבי כליו של לוקח ברשות מוכר כו' דאם קנה אחד מחבירו בשניהן דקנה אחד מהן בממ"נ שאני הכא דהוא ענין דקנסא דהא גופו לא הזיק אלא שורו שהוא ממונו מש"ה הולכין בשניהן להקל עכ"ל הסמ"ע ואין לזה טעם כלל וכבר השיג עליו הב"ח אך מ"ש הב"ח דמיירי בב' בהמות שהזיקו לא נהירא אלא נראה דאף בבהמה אחת כיון דמיבעיא אי אורחא הוא ואין כוונתה להזיק או כוונתה להזיק והוי קרן א"כ י"ל דלמא טבע הבהמה פעמים כך ולפעמים כך. ודלמא בר"ה הזיקה דרך הילוכה כי אורחה ולא היה כונתה להזיק וברשות הניזק היה כונתה להזיק וקרן הוא ודו"ק כן נ"ל ברור. ש"ך:
baer_hetev.en: As a matter of law. This concerns an unresolved question in the Gemara. All agree that if the animal caused damage in the injured party's domain, no payment can be extracted unless the injured party seized the damaging animal itself. He may then collect half damages from its body, because the unresolved doubt permits us to say that the conduct was abnormal and therefore a derivative of horn, and horn pays only half damages from the animal itself. The Tur concludes that even if the same animal damaged the same person once in the public domain and once in the injured party's domain, the law remains the same. The claimant cannot argue: if it is horn, pay me also for the public-domain incident, and if it is foot, pay full damages for the private-domain incident. In both directions we rule leniently for the defendant. The Sema distinguishes this from siman 200 concerning a purchaser's utensils in the seller's domain, where a double doubt may establish acquisition, saying that our case involves a penalty because the owner's own body did not cause the damage, only his ox. This reasoning has no basis, and the Bach already objected. The Bach's proposal that the cases concern two animals is also unconvincing. Rather, even with one animal, since the doubt is whether its act was ordinary and unintentional or deliberate and therefore horn, it is possible that the animal sometimes acts one way and sometimes the other. Perhaps in the public domain it damaged in the course of normal walking without intent, while in the injured party's domain it intended to damage and the act was horn. This is clear. Shach.

כשכשה בזנבה כו' ז"ל הטור אם כשכשה בדרך כל הבהמות (פי' ושיבר' כלי דרך כשכושה) ודאי אורחיה הוא פי' והוי דינו ברגל שפטור על מה שהזיק בר"ה ועל הזיקו ברשו' הניזק חייב נ"ש אבל בכשכש רב (פי' אם הזיק מכח כשכש רב ואי לא הוי מכשכש אלא כדרך שאר הבהמות לא הוי משתבר הכלי) מיבעיא אי הוי כאורח' וכ' הרמב"ם דלא איפשט' לי' אבל הרא"ש כ' דאיפשט' דהוה אורח' והוי תולד' דרגל ואם כשכשה בגיד שלה (ועי"ז שברה הכלי לכ"ע) הוא איבעיא דלא אפשטא כו' ע"ש ועל פי זה נתבאר לך דברי המחב' ומה שכ' מ"ו ר' משה אסרלש ז"ל עליו בהג"ה דהמחב' כ' כדברי הרמב"ם דס"ל דכשכש רב דזנבו וסתם כשכש דגיד שלה שוין הן ושניהן הן איבעיות דלא איפשט' בגמ' אי תולדה דקרן הוא או תולד' דרגל והמע"ה ומ"ה אי לא תפסו הניזק והזיקה בר"ה אין לו כלו' דיכול המזיק לומ' תולדה דרגל הוא ואם הזיקה ברשות הניזק אינו משלם אלא ח"נ ממ"נ אבל אם תפס ונעשה הנזק ברשות הניזק צריך לשלם נ"ש דיד התופס על העליונ' ויאמר תולד' דרגל הוא ואם בר"ה נעשה הנזק יאמר התופס תולדה דקרן הוא וצריך לשלם חצי נזק והיינו דוקא לדעת הרמב"ם דס"ל דמהני תפיסה אף במקום שהוא ספק לנו אי הוה קרן או רגל ועל זה כ' מור"ם די"א (והוא ר"י והרא"ש) דלא מהני תפיס' בספיק' דדינ' ועוד כ' דלדעת הרא"ש אם כשכש בזנבו כשכש (שאינו) רב אפשט' האיבעיא דהוה אורחא ותולדה דרגל היא ואם הזיקה ברשות הרבים פטור לגמרי אפי' למ"ד דמהני תפיסה לספיק' דדינא דכאן אין ספק אלא ודאי אורחא הוא ומינה דאם הזיקה ברשות הניזק דמשלם נזק שלם אפי' לדעת ר"י והרא"ש כיון דודאי אורחא הוא וה"ל למור"ם לכתוב ג"כ צד חיובו דכשכש בזנבו כשכוש שאינו רב ברשות הניזק אלא דחדא באידך תליא וצד החיוב נלמד מצד הפטור כנ"ל:
דבכל ספיקא דדינא לא מהני תפיסה כו'. והיינו בדבר שהוא איבעיא וכנ"ל אבל ג"כ מודים דאם הזיקה ברשו' הניזק דאינו משלם אפי' חצי נזק בלא תפיסה דכיון דלא איפשטא יש לומ' דלא הוה אורחא ותולדה דקרן הוא וקרן אינו משלם חצי נזק אלא מגופו וכמ"ש הטור והמחב' בסימן א' וגם בסימן זה כתבו הטור ע"ש ומ"ה בעינן שיתפוס גופו דהמזיק דוקא וישלם ממנו ח"נ ועד"ר והטור מסיק וכ' בזה ז"ל ואפי' אם היזק לאדם אחד בר"ה וברשות הניזק דינא הכי ואינו יכול לומ' ממ"נ אם תאמר שהוא קרן תתחייב לי גם כן ברה"ר וא"ת שהוא רגל (ומ"ה תפטר על הזיקו בר"ה אם כן) תן לי נזק שלם הזיקו דרשות הניזק אלא בשניהן להקל עד כאן לשון הטור ואע"ג דכתב הטור והמחב' בסי' א' בספיקא דדינא אי כליו של לוקח ברשות מוכר או איפכא קונים וקנה אחד מחבירו בשניהן דקנה בא' מהן ממ"נ שאני הכא דהוא ענין דקנסא דהא גופו לא הזיק אלא שורו שהוא ממונו מ"ה הולכין בשניהן להקל ועד"ר:
meirat_einayim.en:
It swished its tail, etc. The Tur writes: If it swished its tail in the ordinary manner of animals and broke a utensil through that ordinary movement, this is normal conduct and has the law of foot. The owner is exempt for damage in the public domain and liable for full damages in the injured party's domain. If it swished excessively and the utensil would not have broken from ordinary swishing, the Gemara asks whether that remains normal conduct. The Rambam holds the question was not resolved. The Rosh holds it was resolved as normal conduct and therefore a derivative of foot. If it swished with its genital organ and thereby broke a utensil, everyone agrees the Gemara's question remains unresolved. From this one can understand the Mechaber and Rama. The Mechaber follows the Rambam and treats excessive tail swishing and ordinary genital swishing alike as unresolved questions whether they are derivatives of horn or foot. The burden of proof rests upon the claimant. Therefore, if the injured party did not seize and the damage occurred in the public domain, he receives nothing because the tortfeasor can say it was a derivative of foot. If it occurred in the injured party's domain, the tortfeasor pays only half damages whichever way one looks at it. But if the injured party seized, then according to the Rambam, who allows seizure in a legal doubt, his hand is on the upper side. If the damage occurred in the injured party's domain he can say it was a derivative of foot and demand full damages. If it occurred in the public domain he can say it was horn and retain half damages. Rama writes that some say seizure does not help in a doubt of law. He also writes that according to the Rosh, where the tail swishing was not excessive, the question was resolved and it is certainly normal conduct and a derivative of foot. Therefore damage in the public domain is fully exempt even according to one who generally allows seizure in legal doubts. Correspondingly, in the injured party's domain full damages are payable even according to Ri and the Rosh. Rama could have stated the affirmative liability as well, but it follows directly from the exemption.
In every doubt of law, seizure does not help, etc. This refers to an unresolved Talmudic question, as explained above. These authorities nevertheless agree that where the damage occurs in the injured party's domain, even half damages are not collected without seizure, because perhaps the conduct was abnormal and therefore a derivative of horn. Horn pays half damages only from the body of the damaging animal. Thus the injured party must seize the damaging animal itself in order to collect half damages from it. The Tur concludes that even if the same animal damaged one person once in the public domain and once in the injured party's domain, we still rule leniently in both directions. The injured party cannot say: whichever way you characterize the conduct, if it is horn then pay me for the public domain damage as well, and if it is foot then pay me full damages for the damage in my domain. We treat each doubtful penalty leniently. Although in siman 1 the Tur and Mechaber rule that where there is a doubt whether the buyer's utensils acquire in the seller's domain, and the parties made two transactions under opposite circumstances, one of them must have effected acquisition whichever way the law is resolved, that is different. Here we are dealing with a penal obligation, since the owner's own body did not cause the damage but his animal did. Therefore in both doubts we follow the lenient result. See the Derishah.

siftei_kohen.he: וי"א דבכל ספיקא דדינא כו'. וכ"פ מהרש"ל פ' כיצד הרגל סי' ה' וז' ועמ"ש לעיל סי' שפ"ח סעיף א' ועיין בסמ"ע ס"ק ז' עד דהוא ענין דקנסא דהא גופו לא הזיק וכו' אין לזה טעם כלל וכבר השיג עליו הב"ח גם מ"ש הב"ח דמיירי בב' בהמות שהזיקו לא נהירא אלא נראה אף בבהמה אחת כיון דמבעיא אי אורחא היא ואין כוונתה להזיק או כוונתה להזיק והוי קרן א"כ יכול לו' דלמא טבע הבהמה לפעמי' הוא כך ולפעמים כך ודלמא בר"ה הזיקה דרך הלוכה כי אורחא ולא הי' כוונתה להזיק וברשות הניזק היתה כוונת' להזיק וקרן הוא ודוק כן נ"ל ברור:
siftei_kohen.en: And some say that in every unresolved question of law, etc. Maharshal rules likewise in Perek Keitzad HaRegel, simanim 5 and 7. See what I wrote above, siman 388, seif 1. The Sema's explanation that this is a matter of penalty because the person's body did not directly cause the damage has no basis. The Bach already challenged him. Nor is the Bach's limitation to a case involving two animals persuasive. Even with one animal, where the Gemara is uncertain whether this conduct is its ordinary manner, the doubt remains one of liability, and the practical rule follows the principles explained there.

turei_zahav.he: (ס"ה ונתגלגל למקום אמר כו'). דבתר מעיקרא אזלינן ולא ה"ל צרורות אלא גופו וכתב הרא"ש פ' כיצד הרגל דהתיז' ברה"ר והזיקה ברה"י חייבת דאזלי' בתר סוף ואף על גבי דגבי דרסה על כלי ונפל למקום אחר ונשבר אסיקנא לעיל דבתר מעיקרא אזלינן הכא לא אזלינן אלא אחר המקום שנעשה הנזק דגלי קרא ברגל וביער בשדה אחר והביער היה בחצר הניזק עכ"ל וכתב רש"ל וז"ל א"כ דעתו דוקא כשהכל ברשות אז הולכין בתר מעיקרא שהוא ג"כ מקום הניזק וחייב לאפוקי בר"ה לא וא"כ נ"ל צרורות היכי משכחת לה אליביה מאחר שהכל ברשות נימא ניזול בתר מעיקרא ולא יהיה צרורות כמו דרסה על הכלי ונתגלגל למקום אחר אע"כ חילוקא רבה אית ביניהם דלא אמרינן בהו ניזיל בתר מעיקרא אלא כגון שדרסה על הכלי או שזרק כלי מראש הגג שעשה מעיקרא מעשה בגוף הכלי הניזק והיה ראוי לישבר כדמסיק רבה מנא תבירא תבר אבל גבי צרורות לא שייך לומר זיל בתר מעיקרא דבשעת התזה לא היה עדיין ראויה להזיק עד שיגיע למקום אחר לכן אפי' דרסה על הכלי בר"ה והתיזה לרה"י ונשבר פטורה דבתר מעיקרא אזלינן דבתחלת דריסה היה ראויה לשבר משא"כ לפי' הרא"ש שגם בכה"ג חייב עכ"ל ולענ"ד דלא כן הדרך בפי' דברי הרא"ש דדרסה על הכלי בר"ה והתיזה ברה"י דחייב אלא פשיטא דפטור גם לדעת הרא"ש דכיון דאילו נשברה שם היה פטור לא גרע בזה שנשברה ברה"י כיון שהכלי מונח שלא ברשות דבר"ה לא חייבה התורה גבי רגל וזהו עצמו הוא החילוק שחילק הרא"ש בין התיזה בר"ה כו' לנתגלגל ונשבר דבהתיזה בר"ה חייב כיון שהכלי הנשבר הוא מונח ברה"י ברשות ובזה חייבה התורה כיון שהביער בחצר הניזק משא"כ בדרס' בחצר הניזק על הכלי ונתגלגל למקום אחר בחצר הניזק דשם גם במקום הדריסה הוי חצר הניזק בזה אזלינן בתר מעיקרא ומשלם נזק שלם אבל בדרסה על הכלי בר"ה והתיזה לרה"י פטור כיון דהוי הכלי במקום הפקר לגבי ההיזק וכו' ומ"ש רש"ל בזה יש לכוין גם בדעת הרא"ש כן וכ"מ גם בדברי התוס' פ' כיצד הרגל דף יז ד"ה זרק כלי כו' וז"ל וסברא פשוטה היא לחלק בין זורק אבן לזורק כלי עכ"ל ואף על גב דאיתא לקמן סי' שצ"א ס"ז בנוטלת בר"ה ואוכלה ברה"י דחייב שאני התם דהא טלטלה לרה"י והוה כלקחה ברה"י וכמ"ש שם משא"כ כאן שניתז לרה"י:
turei_zahav.en: [Seif 5] And it rolled to another place, the Mechaber says, and so forth. We evaluate the act from its inception, so it is not treated as pebbles but as direct bodily damage. The Rosh writes in the chapter Keitzad HaRegel that if an animal kicked an object in the public domain and it caused damage in the injured party's domain, the owner is liable, because we follow the place where the damage was completed. Although where it stepped on a vessel and the vessel rolled elsewhere and broke we conclude that the law follows the initial act, here we follow the place where the damage occurred, because the verse concerning foot says, “and it consumed in another's field,” and the destruction occurred in the injured party's courtyard. Maharshal understands the Rosh to mean that only where the entire event occurs in an authorized domain do we follow the initial act, which was likewise in the injured party's domain. He therefore asks how the category of pebbles could ever arise according to the Rosh, since whenever everything occurs in an authorized domain we should follow the initial act and treat the damage as direct, as in the case where it stepped on a vessel and the vessel rolled elsewhere. He answers that there is a major distinction. When it stepped on the vessel, or when one threw a vessel from a roof, an act was performed at the outset upon the damaged object itself, and it was already destined to break, as Rabbah says, “he broke an already broken vessel.” With pebbles, however, the projectile was not yet fit to damage at the moment it was kicked until it reached another place. Maharshal therefore concludes that if it stepped on a vessel in the public domain, causing it to fly into the injured party's domain and break there, the owner is exempt because the initial act occurred where the vessel was not protected. In my opinion, this is also the correct understanding of the Rosh. It is obvious that the Rosh would exempt where the animal stepped on the vessel in the public domain and it flew into the private domain. Since the owner would have been exempt had it broken where it was stepped upon, the fact that it ultimately broke in the injured party's domain cannot increase liability, because the vessel was lying in a place where foot is not liable. This is precisely the Rosh's distinction between an object kicked in the public domain and a vessel that rolled and broke elsewhere. In the first case the object that was ultimately damaged was lawfully situated in the injured party's domain, and the Torah imposes liability because the destruction occurred there. In the second case, the animal stepped on a vessel in the injured party's courtyard and it rolled elsewhere within that courtyard. Since the initial act also occurred in the injured party's domain, we follow the inception and impose full damages. But if it stepped on the vessel in the public domain and it flew into the private domain, the owner is exempt because the vessel was initially in an unprotected place. Maharshal's distinction can be understood consistently with the Rosh as well, and Tosafot in Keitzad HaRegel 17b likewise state that it is a simple logical distinction between throwing a stone and throwing a vessel. Although siman 391, seif 7, rules that if an animal takes food in the public domain and eats it in the private domain the owner is liable, that case is different because the animal physically carried the food into the private domain and is considered to have taken it anew there. Here the object merely flew there.

baer_hetev.he: מסיני. פירוש אע"פ שהדברים נראין כסותרין זא"ז שיש לו דין רגל לענין פטור בר"ה ולענין חיוב תשלומין מנכסיו יש לו דין קרן שאינו משלם אלא ח"נ אף ברשות הניזק. מש"ה כת' דהל"מ כן הוא ואין להרהר אחריה. סמ"ע:
baer_hetev.en: From Sinai. Although the rules appear contradictory, since the act has the law of foot for exemption in the public domain but the law of horn regarding payment from the animal's own body, where only half damages are paid even in the injured party's domain, this is a halachah transmitted to Moshe at Sinai and may not be questioned. Sema.

turei_zahav.he: (בססי"ב). על זה כ' הטור ולא נהירא דהאיך יתחייב כו' כ' ב"י דרבינו לא דק ואני אומר דיפה הקשה רבינו דהא ברייתא דקתני בין מלמעלה למטה פטורין ע"כ היינו באיפוכא מיפך כדמשני ר"פ וא"כ הוי חד צד כי אורחיה דהיינו במה שהוא מלמעלה למטה ולחד צד שינוי במה שהוא בהיפך א"כ קשה על הרמב"ם למה כתב חייב נ"ש במלמט' למעלה ולא אפיך דהוה חד בשינוי דהיינו במה שהוא מלמטה למעלה והכי קאמר רבינו דלמה יתחייב בשינוי בחד צד דהיינו במה שהיא ממטה למעלה טפי מאורחא דהיינו מלמעלה למטה דיש שינוי גם כן בחד צד במה דאפכי וצריך לומר דהרמב"ם לא גרס בגמרא מלמעלה למטה פטורין:
turei_zahav.en: At the end of seif 12. The Tur objects: “This is not clear, for how could he become liable?” The Beit Yosef writes that the Tur was imprecise. I say that the Tur's objection is sound. The baraita stating that when the movement is from above downward they are exempt must refer to a reversed movement, as Rav Pappa explains. Thus one aspect follows the ordinary manner, namely movement from above downward, while the other aspect is unusual because the body is inverted. It is therefore difficult why the Rambam rules that one pays full damages when moving from below upward without inversion, for there too one aspect is unusual, namely the upward movement. This is the Tur's point: why should the unusual element of moving upward create greater liability than the ordinary downward movement, where there is also one unusual element because the body is inverted? We must conclude that the Rambam did not have the reading in the Gemara that those moving from above downward are exempt.

ketzot_hachoshen.en: It rolled to another place. Tosafot distinguishes a thrown vessel from a thrown stone or arrow. If one throws a vessel from a roof, the vessel can already be treated as doomed, so another person who breaks it is exempt. But if one shoots an arrow and another person breaks the object before the arrow reaches it, Tosafot says the second person is liable; otherwise the law of half-damages for pebbles would largely disappear. Rosh appears not to accept this distinction. In discussing an animal that kicked pebbles in the public domain and the damage occurred in the injured party's domain, he says we do not follow the beginning of the act there only because Scripture specifically requires the consumption to occur in another's field. If arrows were generally different from thrown vessels, he could have answered simply that pebbles resemble arrows rather than thrown vessels. Tur and the Shulchan Aruch concerning fire likewise imply that where the first person's fire was already sufficient to reach the destination, a second person who adds fuel is not liable. Fire can operate as one's arrows. This suggests that once the first causal force is sufficient, the damage is attributed to that first act. Nimukei Yosef also says that fire as one's arrows is treated as though the entire act occurred when the fire was first released. If the person dies before the fire reaches the stack, his estate remains liable because the act is legally complete from the outset. Tosafot's concern for the law of pebbles can be answered differently. Even if the breakage is regarded as beginning at the first moment, the animal's act remains only damage caused by its force rather than by its body, and the halachah of pebbles can still impose half-damages. This distinction also explains the dispute whether one who actively spreads a fire through an entire building after the first ignition is liable for the additional burning. If fire is treated as one's arrows, the initial ignition can make the later damage legally complete from the outset. Yet Tur says that where a camel spreads the fire through the building it can incur full damages for that spreading, which remains difficult under the strongest version of the initial-act theory. The matter requires study.

meirat_einayim.en: It was walking in the public domain and kicked, etc. Wherever the law mentions pebbles propelled in the normal course, it means pebbles kicked up while walking, a derivative of foot. The owner pays half damages only in the injured party's domain, while in the public domain he is completely exempt, like ordinary foot damage. Whenever pebbles are mentioned together with kicking, however, this is pebbles propelled through an unusual act. Animals commonly walk and thereby scatter pebbles, but they do not ordinarily kick backward with force and thereby send pebbles elsewhere. It was explained above that kicking is an unusual act. The Gemara therefore leaves unresolved whether there is a category of unusual conduct within the law of pebbles. The Rambam understands that the doubt creates both a leniency and a stringency. If there is such an unusual category, then even in the injured party's domain the owner pays only one quarter damages, half of the ordinary half damages for pebbles. Conversely, even in the public domain he pays as for horn, because the act is unusual. If there is no special unusual category for pebbles, the act retains the law of ordinary pebbles, and therefore is exempt in the public domain and liable for half damages in the injured party's domain. Since the Gemara leaves the matter unresolved, the Rambam and Mechaber follow their general position that seizure is effective in a doubtful monetary matter. Accordingly, if the animal kicked and caused damage in the public domain, the owner is exempt because the burden of proof is upon the claimant and perhaps there is no unusual category for pebbles. If the injured party seized property, however, he has the upper hand to say that there is an unusual category and the law is that of horn. Yet once he relies upon that position, he must also accept its lenient side, namely that only one quarter damages is payable. Even that quarter is collectible only from the body of the offending ox, because the liability is then like that of an innocuous horn. This is why the Mechaber concludes that the matter is doubtful. If the kicking caused damage in the injured party's domain, the owner must in any event pay one quarter damages, because even if there is an unusual category for pebbles, that quarter is due. That quarter too is collectible only from the body of the offending animal. If the injured party seized the full half damages, even from other property, it is not removed from him because he may argue that there is no unusual category for pebbles and the case is therefore ordinary foot derived pebbles, for which half damages is payable from all the tortfeasor's property in the injured party's domain.

Roosters are considered forewarned, etc. Until, "and it rolled and broke something, he pays half the damage." This is Rambam's wording, and it is obscure. See Rambam there, where he writes further details concerning a rooster with a cord tied to its leg, distinguishing who tied it and who owned the cord. Raavad objects to most of those rulings. Perhaps for that reason the Mechaber did not copy them. It is nevertheless difficult, because then he should also not have copied this clause, "if it rolled and broke something, he pays half the damage," for Raavad objects to that as well. Nor should Rama have described it as unexplained, since Rambam himself explains it there by writing, "When does this apply," etc.; rather, the other authorities disagree with him. It appears that the Mechaber copied the beginning of Rambam's words because they can be reconciled with the accepted halacha by explaining that the case concerns an ownerless cord and damage caused by throwing. In that case the other authorities also agree that the owner of the rooster pays half the damage, as Rama concludes. Although Rambam himself continues in a way showing that this was not his case, the Mechaber nevertheless chose to quote the portion of his wording that can be sustained. Rama's statement that "it is unexplained" therefore means that the Mechaber copied Rambam's unexplained wording, though this explanation remains forced and requires study.
He pays full damages. Because this is classified as regel.
It threw it and broke something. This is classified as tzerorot.
Only when it propelled an ownerless object. Like tzerorot, which are ownerless.
The owner of the cord is liable. Meaning, for the entire damage if the rooster is ownerless, as Rama concludes, because the owner of the cord should have guarded his cord so that an ownerless rooster would not become entangled in it.
A rolling pit. Meaning, although the owner of the cord did not place it at the location where it caused damage, it nevertheless has the law of a pit, because his cord has the status of a pit that rolled from the place where he left it to the place where it now came to rest through the rooster, and it caused damage there. The Tur writes that if it caused damage after coming to rest, the owner is exempt for damage to utensils, as explained in siman 410 under the law of a pit, where we expound "a donkey" and not utensils. The exclusion of "an ox" and not a person applies specifically where the person dies by falling into the pit, whereas a person will not die from this cord. By contrast, a utensil that breaks has thereby suffered its equivalent of death. If the damage occurs while the object is being dragged or thrown, liability is based on regel or fire, and one is liable for all categories of property.
Both pay together. Because the owner of the rooster was also negligent, since he should have guarded his rooster.
The owner of the rooster pays one quarter. Throwing by a rooster is like tzerorot of an ox, for which only half damages are paid. Since the owner of the cord must share the payment, the rooster's owner bears only half of his own half-liability, namely one quarter of the damage, while the remaining three quarters fall upon the owner of the cord. Had the owner of the cord been the only responsible party, such as where the rooster was ownerless, he would have been obligated for the entire damage.
If it caused damage after coming to rest. We expound, "If a man shall dig a pit," excluding a pit created by an ox. Therefore there is no basis to impose liability upon the owner of the rooster, even if the cord was ownerless and caused damage after coming to rest.
Even if the cord has an owner. This is also the Tur's wording. He could seemingly have stated an even greater novelty, that this applies even if the rooster also has an owner. One must say that he saw no additional novelty in that, because any damage attributable to the rooster certainly falls upon the person who tied the cord to it and not upon the rooster's owner. Once he took the rooster and tied the cord to it, he assumed responsibility for that act. The novelty is only that he is also liable in the capacity of the cord's owner, as owner of the obstacle, even where the liability is not attributed to the rooster itself.
